newsitem.title: GERMANY: GRUNDIG BOARD MEETS AMID SHAKEOUT RUMOURS.
newsitem.headline: GRUNDIG BOARD MEETS AMID SHAKEOUT RUMOURS.

text.p: Top executives at German consumer electronics maker Grundig AG went into a meeting of of its supervisory board on Monday with speculation rife that the troubled company was headed for a management change.

As the meeting got under way at Grundig's base in the southern town of Fuerth, several hundred workers gathered outside management offices to protest against planned job cuts and demand a takeover by the state government of Bavaria.

Labour leaders on the board were planning to seek a no-confidence vote in chief executive Pieter van der Wal, whose turnaround plan called for slashing a third of the loss-making company's 8,500 workers.
They would also seek a vote against supervisory board chief Christian Schwarz-Schilling, Gerd Labodda, an employee representative on the board, told Reuters last week.
A Grundig spokesman said no such vote was scheduled for the meeting, although Van der Wal and Schwarz-Schilling would hold a news conference later on Monday after the session.

Grundig, which lost 250 million marks last year and 600 million in 1995, was set adrift on January 1 when Dutch giant Philips Electronics NV gave up control of the company, ending a costly struggle to revitalize one of Germany's most well known brands of televisions and stereos.
Two weeks ago the IG Metall union called for Bavaria to take temporary control of Grundig to stabilise the firm -- a move Bavarian officials have ruled out.
The union had complained Philips' retreat left a "leadership vacuum" at Grundig, which saw finance chief Karl Heinz Wieland quit January 13.
"If the state doesn't fill the vaccuum, who will?" Lobodda said.
Under Van der Wal, who was hired by Philips less than a year ago, Grundig was seeking new partners and saw a return to profitability in 1998 after cutting the headcount to 6,000.
The company recently said it would shift TV production out of Germany to Austria and sell a video and security systems business to Germany's Plettac AG.
Despite the moves, analysts said they expected the company to lose another 135 million marks this year. Grundig had 1996 sales of about three billion marks.
Philips, which has lost 1.5 billion marks on Grundig since 1984, still owns 32 percent of the company but plans to act as a passive shareholder.
Philips had run the company under an agreement with the Max Grundig Foundation, which owns just under 70 percent of the company.
